lindisfarne.title: The raid on Lindisfarne
lindisfarne.full: The monks of a quiet island priory were singing their morning prayers. Out at sea, long ships with striped sails cut through the grey waves. The year was AD 793, and the island was Lindisfarne, off the coast of Northumbria. The ships carried Vikings from across the North Sea. They ran up the beach and burst into the church. They grabbed silver cups, jewelled books and food. Some monks hid in the fields until the ships sailed away. News of the raid spread across England. People had never seen anything like it. Many say the Viking Age began on that cold June day.
lindisfarne.brief: The bells were still ringing for morning prayers when the lookout saw sails on the horizon. The wind smelled of salt and seaweed. Nobody on the little island knew who was coming, or why. By lunchtime, nothing there would ever be the same again.
lindisfarne.pictureAlt: Longships with striped sails land on a rocky island beach beside a small stone church.

questions.hint: Look for who the ships carried across the North Sea.
The story names the island off Northumbria.

tutankhamun.title: Tutankhamun's tomb
tutankhamun.full: Sand blew across the dry hills as the workers dug. For years they had found nothing but rubble. Then, in November AD 1922, a boy uncovered a stone step. The step led down to a sealed door. Howard Carter, an English archaeologist, had searched this place for many seasons. He was digging in the Valley of the Kings, near Luxor in Egypt. Pharaohs had been buried here more than three thousand years before. Carter made a small hole in the door and held up a candle. Gold glinted everywhere in the flickering light. Lord Carnarvon, who paid for the dig, asked if he could see anything. "Yes, wonderful things," Carter replied. Inside lay the tomb of the boy king Tutankhamun. It was the most complete royal tomb ever found.
tutankhamun.brief: A hot wind swept dust across the rocky hills. Workers with baskets had dug here for years and found only stones. Their leader was running out of money and hope. One more winter, he decided, would be the last. Then a shout rang out from a trench. Someone had found a step cut into the rock, leading down into the dark.
tutankhamun.pictureAlt: An archaeologist holds a candle up to a small hole in a sealed stone doorway, with gold glinting beyond.

questions.hint: Look for the archaeologist who held up the candle.
The story names the place where pharaohs were buried.

boudica.title: Boudica's revolt
boudica.full: The Iceni people of eastern Britain were furious. Roman soldiers had seized their land and treated their royal family cruelly. Their queen, Boudica, would not stay quiet. In AD 60 she gathered a huge army of Britons. Tribes joined her from all around. They marched towards Camulodunum, the Roman town we now call Colchester. Most Roman soldiers were far away in Wales. The town had no strong walls to protect it. Boudica's warriors swept through the streets. The settlers hid in the great temple of Emperor Claudius. After two days, the temple fell too. The whole town was burned to the ground. Today, archaeologists still find a red layer of ash beneath Colchester's streets.
boudica.brief: Smoke drifted over the fields as chariots rumbled along the track. Thousands of angry warriors marched behind them, banging shields and shouting. They had been insulted, and now they wanted revenge. Ahead lay a busy town full of new buildings and frightened families. Its people had no walls to hide behind. Messengers galloped away for help, but help was very far away.
boudica.pictureAlt: A woman with long red hair rides a chariot at the front of a crowd of warriors towards a town.

great_fire.title: The Great Fire of London
great_fire.full: Early on a Sunday in September AD 1666, a fire began in a bakery on Pudding Lane. The baker, Thomas Farriner, escaped through an upstairs window. A strong east wind pushed the flames from roof to roof. The wooden houses of London burned like dry sticks. Samuel Pepys, a navy official, watched from a boat on the River Thames. That night he wrote about the fire in his famous diary. He saw people throwing their belongings into boats. He even buried his best cheese in the garden to save it. The fire burned for four days. Soldiers blew up houses to stop it spreading. Old St Paul's Cathedral was destroyed. Thousands of families lost their homes, but very few people died.
great_fire.brief: It was a hot, dry summer, and the wooden houses leaned close together. A strong wind was blowing from the east. In the dark streets, everyone was fast asleep. Then a smell of smoke crept under the doors. Somewhere nearby, an oven had not been put out properly. By morning, bells were ringing and people were running for the river with whatever they could carry.
great_fire.pictureAlt: Flames rise over crowded wooden houses at night while people row boats full of belongings across a river.

hastings.title: The Battle of Hastings
hastings.full: On 14 October AD 1066, two armies faced each other on a hill in southern England. King Harold's tired English soldiers stood at the top behind a wall of shields. They had marched all the way from a battle in the north. At the bottom waited William of Normandy and his knights on horseback. William had sailed across the Channel to claim the English crown. The fighting near Hastings lasted all day. Arrows flew and horses charged up the slope. Late in the afternoon, Harold was killed. The English army broke apart and fled. On Christmas Day, William was crowned king in Westminster Abbey. Later, people called him William the Conqueror.
hastings.brief: Two tired armies stood facing each other as the sun came up. One waited at the top of a slope, shields locked together. The other had crossed the sea in hundreds of boats, bringing horses and archers. Both leaders believed the crown was theirs. By nightfall only one of them would still be alive, and a whole country would have a new ruler.
hastings.pictureAlt: Knights on horseback charge up a grassy hill towards a line of soldiers holding round shields.

questions.hint: Look for who sailed across the Channel.

The date is at the very start of the story.

skara_brae.title: Skara Brae
skara_brae.full: A cold wind blew off the sea as a family woke in their stone house. Their home had beds, shelves and a hearth, all made from flat stones. The house sat among a few others, joined by low covered passages. This village was Skara Brae, on Orkney in the far north of Scotland. The people living there were Stone Age farmers. They kept cattle and sheep and grew barley in small fields. They fished in the sea and gathered shellfish from the beach. They had no metal tools, only stone, bone and wood. Around 3000 BC, life here was busy and safe. Thousands of years later, a great storm blew the sand away and uncovered the village.
skara_brae.brief: Wind howled over the low green hills and waves crashed on the beach. Inside a snug stone home, a fire crackled in the middle of the floor. Children slept on beds piled with soft furs and heather. Outside, the cattle huddled together against the cold. Nobody here had ever travelled far from home, and nobody wanted to tonight.
skara_brae.pictureAlt: A small stone house with a fire in the middle, stone beds and shelves, and a family sitting round the hearth.

questions.hint: Look for who kept cattle and grew barley.
The story names the village on Orkney.
Find the date with BC in it.

olympia.title: The first Olympic Games
olympia.full: Crowds gathered in a green valley beside a sacred grove of olive trees. They had come to honour Zeus, king of the gods. This place was Olympia, in southern Greece. The year was 776 BC, and the very first Olympic Games were about to begin. There was only one race, a sprint along a straight track. The runners were Ancient Greeks from many different cities. They ran barefoot over the hot sand. A young cook named Koroibos crossed the line first. His prize was not a medal. Instead, he was given a crown made of olive leaves. Later Games added wrestling, chariot races and the long jump. Wars between cities stopped so athletes could travel safely.
olympia.brief: Thousands of people crowded around a long, dusty track. The sun was blazing, and the air smelled of olive trees and smoke from the altars. At one end, a line of young men stood ready, barefoot and nervous. Nobody had seen a contest quite like this before. The crowd fell silent, waiting for the signal to run.
olympia.pictureAlt: Barefoot runners sprint along a sandy track while a crowd watches from a grassy bank beside olive trees.

The story names the place in southern Greece.

hadrians_wall.title: Hadrian's Wall
hadrians_wall.full: In AD 122, Emperor Hadrian visited the far edge of his empire in Britain. He was worried about raids from the tribes living further north. So he ordered his soldiers to build a great wall. It stretched seventy-three miles across northern England, from coast to coast. The soldiers cut and carried thousands of heavy stones. Every mile they built a small fort with a gate. Bigger forts, like Housesteads, held hundreds of men. Soldiers came from all over the empire, even from Syria and Spain. They kept watch through freezing winters. Traders and families settled in villages beside the forts. The wall took about six years to finish. You can still walk along parts of it today.
hadrians_wall.brief: Icy rain blew sideways across the bare hills. A line of men in metal helmets heaved another heavy stone into place. Their hands were raw and their feet were frozen. Far from their warm homes, they grumbled about the cold and the mud. Beyond the hills lived fierce tribes who did not want them there. Every day the great line of stone grew a little longer.
hadrians_wall.pictureAlt: Soldiers in helmets lift stones onto a long wall that winds over green hills in the rain.

questions.hint: Look for who ordered the soldiers to build.
